title: Jerusalem Falls, Then a Door Opens
overview: Judah's last four kings fall under foreign powers until Babylon destroys Jerusalem and its temple, and the chapter closes with a Persian king letting the exiles go home.

parts.label: A king Egypt removed (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: After King Josiah died fighting Egypt, the people crowned his son Jehoahaz, but Egypt's king Necho deposed him within three months, took him to Egypt and charged Judah a heavy payment. Necho then put another son on the throne and renamed him Jehoiakim, a way of showing who really held power.

parts.label: Babylon takes control (vv. 5-10)
parts.note: Babylon soon replaced Egypt as Judah's master, and Nebuchadnezzar carried off Jehoiakim's son Jehoiachin along with precious objects from God's temple, placing them in his own god's temple. Some Hebrew copies give Jehoiachin's age as eight, but 2 Kings says eighteen, and most scholars see the lower number as a copying slip.

parts.label: Zedekiah and ignored warnings (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: Zedekiah broke the loyalty oath he had sworn to Babylon in God's name and ignored the prophet Jeremiah, while priests and people brought other nations' worship practices into the temple. The writer stresses that God kept sending messengers out of pity, and that mocking them is what finally left no remedy.

parts.label: Jerusalem destroyed (vv. 17-19)
parts.note: Babylon's army killed young and old without mercy, even inside the temple, then looted it, burned it and tore down the city walls, around 587 or 586 BC. The writer openly presents this slaughter as God's judgment carried out through Babylon and does not soften it.

parts.label: Exile and the land's rest (vv. 20-21)
parts.note: Israel's law said farmland should rest unplanted every seventh year, and the writer sees the emptied land as finally receiving the rests it had been denied. The seventy years come from Jeremiah's prophecy, and scholars debate whether it is an exact count or a round number for a lifetime.

parts.label: Cyrus lets them return (vv. 22-23)
parts.note: After Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC, its king Cyrus allowed exiled peoples to return home, and here he names the LORD as the one who charged him to rebuild the temple. In the traditional Jewish order of the Bible this is the very last passage, so the whole collection ends with an invitation to go up to Jerusalem.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether to read Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem as God directly sending judgment, as the writer states, or as the writer's faith-shaped way of making sense of a national catastrophe.
think: When a disaster follows years of warnings that went unheeded, how do you sort out what came from people's own choices and what came from forces no one could control?
